summary: Suggests a mechanism by which a user process can attach itself to the local SNMP agent on a host to implement portions of the MIB. The mechanism is local to the host. It was Experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes a way for a program on a machine to contribute its own objects to the network management system. The program registers the branch of the object tree it wants to own, and the local management agent passes any request for those objects to it. Everything happens inside one host, over a local connection.

questions: how does smux register a mib subtree
how does a smux peer register a mib subtree
subtitle: A way for a program on a host to add its own objects to the local SNMP agent.

tldr.problem: The SNMP agent on a host is usually a program of its own, reading the kernel to answer questions about the machine. When another program, such as a routing daemon, wants to publish its own managed objects, the two have no way to talk.
tldr.mechanism: The program registers a branch of the management tree with the local agent over a local TCP connection, and the agent then forwards management requests for that branch to the program and passes the answers back.
tldr.outcome: The agent can be kept small and a vendor can ship management support in a separate program. The document was an Experimental protocol and is now Historic.

facts.label: Registration priority range
facts.value: 0 to 2147483647, lower value means higher priority

today: RFC 1227 was published in May 1991 as an Experimental Protocol for the Internet community, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its status is Historic.

sections.title: Why a Multiplexing Protocol Is Needed
sections.content:
On typical kernel and user systems, an agent speaking SNMP is often implemented as a user process that reads kernel variables in order to realize the Internet-standard MIB. This approach works fine as long as all of the information needed by the SNMP agent resides in either the kernel or in stable storage, meaning files. However, when other user processes are employed to implement other network services, such as routing protocols, communication between the SNMP agent and those processes is problematic.

The SNMP multiplexing protocol, SMUX, is introduced to solve this. When a user process, termed a SMUX peer, wishes to export a MIB module, it initiates a SMUX association to the local SNMP agent, registers itself, and later fields management operations for objects in the MIB module.

Carrying the approach to its fullest, it is possible to generalize the SNMP agent so that it knows about only the SNMP group of the Internet-standard MIB, with all other portions implemented by another process. The RFC calls this quite useful, for example, when a computer manufacturer wishes to provide SNMP access for its operating system in binary form. In addition to defining the SMUX protocol, the document defines a MIB for the SMUX, which must also be implemented in the local SNMP agent.

The status of the document is stated at the top: it suggests a mechanism by which a user process may associate itself with the local SNMP agent on a host in order to implement portions of the MIB, and that mechanism would be local to the host. It is an Experimental Protocol for the Internet community, and discussion and suggestions for improvement are requested.
sections.plainLanguage: The management agent is one program; the information it reports is often produced by others. The RFC proposes that those other programs register their part of the object tree with the agent, and the agent then acts as a front desk for them.

sections.title: Two Ways to Plug a MIB into an Agent
sections.content:
There are two approaches to integrating arbitrary MIB modules with the SNMP agent. In the request-response model, the SNMP requests received by the agent are simply propagated to the user process that exported the MIB module. The SMUX peer performs the operation and returns a response, and in turn the agent propagates that response back to the network management station. This model is said to be agent-driven, since after registration the SNMP agent initiates all transactions.

The cache-ahead model requires that the SMUX peer, after registration, periodically updates the SNMP agent with the subtree for the MIB module that has been registered. When the agent receives an SNMP request for information retrieval, it locally performs the operation and returns a response to the network management station; SNMP set requests are given immediately to the SMUX peer. This model is said to be peer-driven, since after registration the SMUX peer initiates all transactions.

Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages, and the architecture envisioned supports both in the following fashion: the protocol between the SNMP agent and the SMUX peer is based on the request-response model. However, the SMUX peer may itself be a user process which employs the cache-ahead model with other user processes. Such a peer acts as a firewall for those user processes which actually implement the managed objects in the given MIB module. The document describes only the SMUX protocol for the request-response model; each SMUX peer is free to define a cache-ahead protocol specific to the application at hand.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the agent asks the program for every value, or the program keeps the agent's copy up to date. The RFC's own protocol is the first kind, but a peer that wants the second can sit in the middle and do it for the programs beneath it.

sections.title: The SMUX Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol is simple. The SNMP agent listens for incoming connections. Upon establishing a connection, the SMUX peer issues an OpenPDU to initialize the SMUX association. If the SNMP agent declines the association, it issues a ClosePDU and closes the connection; if it accepts, no response is issued by the agent at all.

For each subtree defined in a MIB module that the peer wishes to register or unregister, the peer issues a RReqPDU, and the agent answers with a corresponding RRspPDU. The agent returns RRspPDUs in the same order as the RReqPDUs were received.

When the peer wishes to issue a trap it issues an SNMP TrapPDU, and the agent propagates this to the network management stations that it is configured to send traps to.

When the agent receives an SNMP GetRequest-PDU, GetNextRequest-PDU or SetRequest-PDU which includes one or more variable-bindings within a subtree registered by a peer, the agent sends an equivalent SNMP PDU containing only those variables within the subtree registered by that peer. The peer applies the indicated operation and issues a corresponding SNMP GetResponse-PDU, and the agent then correlates this result and propagates the resulting GetResponse-PDU to the network management station.

When either the agent or the peer wishes to release the association, the ClosePDU is issued, the connection is closed, and all subtree registrations for that association are released.
sections.plainLanguage: The sequence is short. The program connects and says hello; if the agent refuses, it says so and hangs up. The program then asks to own a branch of the tree, and the agent answers. From then on, a management request that touches that branch is passed to the program, and its answer is passed back.

sections.title: Registration, Priorities and Two-Phase Commit
sections.content:
Associated with each registration is an integer priority, from 0 to (2^31) minus 1; the lower the value, the higher the priority. Multiple peers may register the same subtree, but they must do so at different priorities, so that a subtree and a priority uniquely identify a peer. If a peer wishes to register a subtree at a priority that is already taken, the agent repeatedly increments the integer value until an unused priority is found. The special priority -1 may be used when registering a subtree, and selects the highest available priority. The agent may also select an arbitrarily worse priority for a peer, based on local configuration information.

When a subtree is registered, the peer with the highest registration priority is exclusively consulted for all operations on that subtree. Agents must enforce the subtree mounting effect, which hides the registrations by other peers of objects within the subtree. The RFC's example is that if a peer registered "sysDescr" and later another peer registered "system", which scopes "sysDescr", then all requests for "sysDescr" would be given to the latter peer. An agent should disallow any attempt to register above, at, or below the SNMP and SMUX subtrees of the MIB, and other subtrees may be disallowed as an implementation-specific option. A peer may remove registrations only for those subtrees it has registered; if the priority in the RReqPDU is -1, the registration of highest priority is selected for deletion, and otherwise only that registration with the precise priority is selected.

Atomic sets use a simple two-phase commit protocol between the agent and the peers. When an SNMP SetRequest-PDU is received, the agent determines which peers will participate in the transaction, and for each of them at least one SNMP SetRequest-PDU is sent, with only those variables of interest to that peer. Each peer must either accept or refuse the set operation, without actually performing it. A peer that accepts sends back an SNMP GetResponse-PDU with an error-status of noError(0); a peer that refuses returns one with a non-zero error-status. The agent examines all of the responses: if at least one peer refused, a SMUX SOutPDU with value rollback is sent to each peer, telling it to discard any knowledge of the requested operation; otherwise, if all peers accepted, a SMUX SOutPDU with value commit is sent to each peer, telling it to perform the operation. In either case the peer does not generate a response to the SOutPDU.

Two further details concern how requests are built. When constructing a GetRequest-PDU or GetNextRequest-PDU for a peer, the agent may send one or more variables in a single request, and in all cases should process each variable sequentially, blocking accordingly when a peer is contacted. And the request_id field takes a special meaning: if the agent generates multiple PDUs for a peer from a single PDU received from the management station, then the request_id of the PDUs sent to the peer must take the same value, which need bear no relationship to the request_id of the PDU originally received by the agent.

The get-next operator needs care. Each peer acts as though it contains the entire MIB when processing a GetNext-PDU from the agent. The agent must therefore check each variable returned in the GetResponse-PDU to ensure it is still within the same registered subtree that caused the GetNext-PDU to be sent to that peer. For each variable that is not, the agent must include it in a GetNext-PDU to the peer for the succeeding registered subtree, until responses are available for all variables within their expected registered subtree.
sections.plainLanguage: Two programs may both want the same branch of the tree, so each registration carries a priority number, lower meaning preferred, and only the preferred program is asked. When a management station sets several variables at once, the agent asks each interested program whether it can do it and only tells them to go ahead if all of them say yes; otherwise it tells them all to forget it.

sections.title: The Transport and the MIB for SMUX
sections.content:
The SMUX protocol may be mapped onto any connection-mode transport service, and at present only one such mapping is defined. When TCP provides the transport backing, the SNMP agent listens on TCP port 199. Each SMUX PDU is serialized using the Basic Encoding Rules and sent on the TCP, and because ASN.1 objects are self-delimiting when encoded using BER, no packetization protocol is required.

The MIB objects for the SMUX are implemented by the local SNMP agent, and live under smux, which is { unix 4 }. The smuxPeerTable has one entry per peer, with smuxPindex, an index that uniquely identifies a peer, smuxPidentity, the authoritative designation for a peer, smuxPdescription, a human-readable description of at most 255 characters, and smuxPstatus, which takes the values valid(1), invalid(2) or connecting(3). Setting that last object to invalid(2) has the effect of invalidating the corresponding entry in the table; whether the agent then removes the entry is an implementation-specific matter, so management stations must be prepared to receive tabular information corresponding to entries not currently in use and must examine the relative status object to interpret them correctly.

The smuxTreeTable records what is registered, with smuxTsubtree, the MIB subtree being exported by a peer, smuxTpriority, the peer's priority for that subtree, smuxTindex, the peer's identity, and smuxTstatus, which takes the values valid(1) or invalid(2) and works the same way as the peer table's status object.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything happens over a local TCP connection on port 199. The agent keeps two tables: one listing the programs that have registered, and one listing what each of them has claimed to own, so that a manager can see both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section of the memo is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The one piece of authentication in the protocol is worth noting in that light. The OpenPDU has a choice of one form, SimpleOpen, which carries a version number, the identity of the peer as an object identifier, an implementation-specific description, and a password field. The comment in the definition records that a zero length password indicates no authentication, so the mechanism is present but optional, and the mechanism itself is described in the document as currently only simple authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. The opening message can carry a password, but the definition says that a zero-length password means no authentication at all, so the mechanism is there but optional.

messages.label: OpenPDU
messages.note: Initializes the association. The agent either closes the connection or accepts it silently.

messages.label: RReqPDU
messages.note: Asks to register a subtree, with a priority.

messages.label: RRspPDU
messages.note: The priority granted, or failure. Responses come back in the order the requests were sent.

messages.label: GetRequest-PDU
messages.note: A management request naming objects in the registered subtree.

messages.label: GetRequest-PDU
messages.note: Only the variables within the subtree this peer registered.

messages.label: GetResponse-PDU
messages.note: The peer applies the operation and returns the values.

messages.label: GetResponse-PDU
messages.note: The agent correlates the result and passes it back.

viz.caption: THE TWO MODELS FOR CONNECTING A MIB TO AN AGENT

cells: The agent forwards the request to the peer and waits.
The peer pushes the subtree to the agent periodically.
Forwarded to the peer in the transaction.
This is the model the RFC specifies.
A peer may use it with the processes beneath it, acting as a firewall.

viz.caption: THE SMUX PROTOCOL DATA UNITS AND THEIR TAGS

items.label: OpenPDU
items.desc: Sent by the peer immediately after the TCP connection is open. Carries a version, the peer identity, a description and an optional password.

items.label: ClosePDU
items.desc: Used by either side immediately before the TCP connection is closed. Releasing the association also releases its registrations.

items.label: RReqPDU
items.desc: Register or unregister a subtree: the subtree, a priority, and whether to delete, add read-only or add read-write.

items.label: RRspPDU
items.desc: The agent's answer to a registration request: the granted priority, or failure.

items.label: SOutPDU
items.desc: The second phase of the two-phase commit: commit or rollback.
